paras: The lynching of James Foster was the hanging of a Black man, James Foster, by a mounted mob that took him from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, late on the night of Sunday, June 10, 1888. Foster had been arrested three days earlier on a charge of criminally assaulting the eight-year-old daughter of John Howard, and the mob hanged him from a tree outside the town. The story ran widely as an Evansville wire; a Henderson correspondent added that part of the mob were Black men and that it nearly lynched a second prisoner.

Foster was arrested on Thursday morning, June 7, at the instance of John Howard, charged with a criminal assault upon Howard's "little eight-year-old daughter" a few miles from Henderson in the country. According to the Evansville dispatch, he "strenuously denied his guilt," but "conclusive evidence" was said to have been found on his clothing, which was "stained with blood." An earlier mob, the dispatch said, came in from the country on Sunday night but went home after finding Jailer Johnson "on the alert."
The Henderson jail also held Dave Braxton, a Black man tried in Hopkinsville on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. Patzke, and moved to Henderson to escape lynching.

A Henderson dispatch to the Washington Critic said that at 11:55 p.m. "a well-armed and organized mob" of about sixty mounted men, "a part of whom were negroes," approached the jail quietly, captured Jailer Johnson and made him give up the keys. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian's version, timed at 11:45, added that the men were "closely masked" and placed the police under arrest "for the time being."

The Evansville wire told it differently: at midnight two hundred armed Kentuckians on horseback rushed the jail before the jailer was fully alarmed, broke down the cell door and carried Foster off in a vehicle. In that version Foster begged for his life along the road and "told all manner of stories to prove his innocence," and the mob hanged him from an oak in the woods where the assault was said to have taken place.

The Critic's correspondent, warned off with revolvers, later viewed the body hanging from a limb about a mile from the jail, hands and feet tied. Afterward the mob voted on whether to return to the jail and lynch Braxton; the vote was close, and the men dispersed.

No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action appears in the coverage. On Wednesday, June 13, Braxton attacked turnkey James Turner in what a Henderson special called a jail-break attempt, and Turner shot him through the lung. The South Kentuckian headlined it "Dave Braxton Killed," though the dispatch said only that the wound was "pronounced fatal."

The Evansville wire carried the story across the country, appearing on June 11 in the Washington Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette, on June 12 in the New York Sun, and as late as June 19 in the Atlanta Constitution. Headlines named the charge and the victim's race, as in "Ravisher Lynched" (Alexandria Gazette) and "A Negro Assaulter Lynched" (San Antonio Daily Light).

Several papers openly approved: the Critic headlined its report "A Wretch Strung Up" and ended it by saying Foster "richly deserved his fate," and the Maysville Evening Bulletin called the hanging a "Necktie Party With a Lecherous Brute." The Mitchell Capital in Dakota headlined it "Hung Where He Should Be."
Kentucky papers such as the Stanford Interior Journal and The Climax stressed a detail the wire omitted, that the mob was "composed partly of negroes."
Accounts differed on the size of the mob: about sixty in the Henderson dispatch, two hundred in the Evansville wire, and forty in a Big Sandy News headline set over wire text that said two hundred.

On Foster's guilt, the Henderson correspondent said he confessed, while the wire said he denied the charge to the end; no account from Foster's side appears. The girl's race was also reported both ways: the Henderson dispatch and the Interior Journal called her "colored," while an Evening Star headline spoke of a "white child" and the Cambria Freeman of "a little white girl named Howard."

reader.title: Lynching of James Foster
bases: A mounted mob took Foster, a jailed Black man charged with assault, from the Henderson jail and hanged him (A1, A4, A6).

Every account has a mob of forty to two hundred men seizing Foster from jail and hanging him without trial (A1, A4, A16); the papers tied it to the assault charge and to 'swift Kentucky justice' (A7, A22).
A Henderson correspondent's dispatch (A1, A6) and the separate Evansville wire (A4, A7) agree that Foster was taken from the Henderson jail by a mob and hanged, though they differ on details.

accounts.gist: About sixty masked, mounted men, part of them Black, captured the jailer, hanged Foster a mile from the jail, voted narrowly to spare Braxton; says Foster confessed.

accounts.label: Evansville wire
accounts.gist: Two hundred armed Kentuckians rushed the jail at midnight, broke in, and hanged Foster at the scene of the alleged crime; says he denied guilt but bloodstained clothing was 'conclusive evidence'.

framing.detail: The Critic headlined 'A Wretch Strung Up' and said Foster 'richly deserved his fate'; the Maysville Bulletin called it a 'Necktie Party With a Lecherous Brute'.
Most papers ran the Evansville wire under headlines such as 'Ravisher Lynched' and 'A Kentucky Lynching'.
The Mitchell Capital headlined 'Hung Where He Should Be' and 'Swift Kentucky Justice'.

conflicts.note: The Henderson dispatch is the local source; the Big Sandy News headline contradicts its own text.
